design_detail: Invited-style commentary (Addiction 2011;106:787-788), single author, published alongside Halpern et al. (2011). Four running-text paragraphs, a declaration of interests and 18 references; no sections, methods or data. Argues that Halpern et al.'s study, designed to limit confounding by other drug use, strengthens the case against functionally significant serotonergic neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy, and that the one difference found is compatible with pre-existing traits. Locators count the four paragraphs from the start of the text.
can_establish: What the author argues about Halpern et al. (2011) and about pre-existing traits as an explanation for test differences, and which studies he cites for it.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy does or does not cause lasting serotonergic damage: the commentary adds no data, and its central argument (pre-drug traits) is offered as a possibility.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The study discussed is Halpern et al. (2011): people who used ecstasy, selected for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol, and non-using controls recruited from the same rave subculture (1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the author chooses the studies discussed.
sample.selection_effects: The commentary cites the null and pre-trait side of the literature and the author's own earlier critiques (refs 2, 7, 11); it does not discuss the PET studies of the serotonin transporter published from 2008 to 2010 that the other letters in this batch cite (McCann et al., 2008; Kish et al., 2010).

exposure.measurement: Not described in the commentary beyond the selection of the Halpern et al. sample for low exposure to other drugs.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not given; the commentary refers only to heavy and moderate subgroups.
exposure.polysubstance: Presented as the study's main strength: the ecstasy group was selected for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol, unlike most studies, in which confounding by other substances could not be ruled out (1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: As described: non-using controls who belonged to the rave subculture like the ecstasy group (1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: As described: analyses adjusted for demographic and other factors, for example attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The commentary's central point: impulsivity, weaker executive control and lower serotonergic function before any drug use may predispose to heavier drug use, so the people who used most heavily would on average be more impulsive even without neurotoxicity (2nd and 3rd paragraphs). It cites one prospective study in which test performance in people who had not used ecstasy predicted later first use (ref 12).

outcomes.instruments: As described: a battery of 15 neuropsychological tests, of which the Revised Strategy Application Test (RSAT) is the only one discussed (1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The commentary notes that poor RSAT performance in people with brain injury has been read as deficient prefrontal inhibitory control over reward-driven responding (2nd paragraph, ref 8).
outcomes.operationalization: A clear indication of poorer performance is not defined; no p values or effect sizes are given.

analysis.selective_reporting: Reports only the RSAT difference in the heavier subgroup. It does not mention the non-dominant-hand pegboard difference in the same subgroup, which in Halpern et al.'s Table 3 has the same p value (0.003), or the overall-group differences on five tests at p of 0.05 or below (checked by this reader in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Tables 2 and 3); Halpern et al. themselves call the RSAT result their only consistently significant finding and the pegboard result likely due to chance.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the commentary does not say how large an effect the study could have detected.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The commentary's evidence is one cross-sectional study with few differences, an argument that pre-existing traits could explain the one it discusses, an analogy with fenfluramine, a cross-sectional comparison read as recovery of transporter binding after abstinence, and two within-person studies of controlled exposure described as finding no deficits without sample sizes or designs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The commentary calls Halpern et al. possibly the most informative retrospective study to date and concludes that, once controlled within-person studies are replicated, MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy may be shown to be a "chimera" (4th paragraph), with Halpern et al.'s findings already supporting that outcome. A null result in a sample of 52 (22 in the heavier subgroup), without effect sizes, is presented as support for absence of harm, and the within-person evidence cited is a conference abstract (ref 17) and a small therapy pilot trial (ref 18).

timeline.event: Critique of the 2004 pilot study by the same author (Lyvers and Hasking, 2004), cited as ref 2.
Halpern et al. (2011), the study discussed.
Letter reading the same study as consistent with neurotoxicity.

replication.where_it_stands: Opposite reading of the same data to Parrott (2011). The argument from pre-existing traits is plausible but untested in this commentary; the within-person exposure studies it relies on are few and small.

funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Bond University, Gold Coast, Australia. The author had criticized the 2004 pilot study (ref 2) and cites three of his own papers (refs 2, 7, 11).

what_would_settle_it: Prospective within-person studies that measure cognition and serotonin transporter binding before and after exposure, large enough to exclude small effects, both in clinical-trial participants and in people who start using ecstasy on their own, with a retested non-using control group.

domains.note: A commentary; no search, studies chosen by the author.
Halpern et al.'s design is appraised; the within-person studies and the fenfluramine imaging study are not.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 18 references are the author's own, including his critique of the pilot study.
The pre-trait argument is offered as a possibility, but the closing paragraph treats absence of evidence as support for absence of harm.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against functionally significant serotonergic neurotoxicity
domains.note: Under-represented: the transporter imaging studies, the pegboard difference and the other overall-group differences in the study discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The commentary is a well-argued statement of the confounding problem in cross-sectional studies, and may be cited for that argument and for what it says about Halpern et al.'s design. It should not be cited as evidence that ecstasy is free of lasting effects.

key_findings.finding: Of the 15 tests in Halpern et al. (2011), chosen because other studies had reported differences on them, the author counts only the Revised Strategy Application Test as clearly poorer, in the heavier subgroup but not the moderate one, compared with controls. He credits the study with selecting people for low exposure to other drugs and alcohol, recruiting controls from the same rave subculture and adjusting for demographic factors and childhood ADHD, and calls it possibly the most informative retrospective study to date.

The author argues that lower strategy-application performance in the heavier subgroup fits pre-drug traits: low serotonergic function has been linked to impulsivity, which is linked to low prefrontal activation, reward sensitivity, signs of frontal dysfunction and heavier substance use; and a prospective study found that test performance in people who had not yet used ecstasy predicted later first use (ref 12, Schilt et al., 2009, on decision making).
key_findings.note: The prospective study is described in one sentence; it was not read here.

key_findings.finding: The author states that the evidence for functional signs of serotonergic neurotoxicity remains mixed (refs 4-7, 13), and that transporter deficiencies in people who use ecstasy appear to recover with abstinence (ref 16, Thomasius et al., 2003), unlike those reported years after fenfluramine (ref 15). He argues that the same traits attributed by some to neurotoxicity may predispose to heavier use, and that retrospective studies cannot separate the two.
key_findings.note: Ref 16 compared people currently using and people who had stopped, at one time point, as Parrott (2013, p. 11 of the in-press PDF) describes it; the recovery is a cross-sectional inference.

key_findings.finding: The author proposes within-person comparisons before and after controlled experimental exposure as the way to resolve the question, states that the few examples so far found no deficits (ref 17, Ludewig et al., 2003, a conference abstract; ref 18, Mithoefer et al., 2010, a pilot randomized trial in PTSD), and concludes that Halpern et al.'s findings support the view that MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy may prove illusory.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary says only the strategy-application test clearly differed in the heavier subgroup, but in Halpern et al.'s Table 3 the non-dominant-hand pegboard difference in that subgroup has the same p value (0.003); Halpern et al. judged it likely chance on exploratory analyses (checked in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Table 3 and Discussion, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's results are presented as cleaner than its tables show; claims should cite the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Recovery of transporter binding with abstinence is cited to a study that compared people currently using and people who had stopped, at a single time point (ref 16), not to repeated scans of the same people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The recovery statement is open to the same selection problems as other cross-sectional comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The within-person evidence (refs 17-18) is a conference abstract in a journal supplement and a small pilot trial; neither sample size nor whether any neurotoxicity measure was taken is stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that controlled exposure has not produced deficits cannot be weighed from the commentary.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.03344.x (free access; all four paragraphs, declaration of interests, author affiliation and the 18 references read in this reader's own browser tab). Statements about Halpern et al. (2011) were checked against its PMC full text (PMC3053129).
